papers.title: The temporal dynamics of same vs. different relational integration in the adult brain
papers.abstract: Humans readily abstract common relations across situations that look entirely different. For example, when reading a map, we align relations between landmarks on a screen with those in the world around us. Relational comparison forms the basis of analogical reasoning. Here, we investigated how recognising same and different relations instantiated by various simple shapes unfolds in the brain over time. We recorded EEG from adults (N = 20) viewing shape pairs presented in a periodic visual oddball paradigm, in which exemplars of one relation occurred at regular intervals within a stream of the other (e.g., same-same-same-different or vice versa). Frequency-domain analysis revealed robust responses at the stimulation rate (2.5 Hz) and the oddball rate (0.625 Hz), providing an implicit neural measure of relational discrimination. Time-resolved decoding showed that same and different could be decoded while holding Sequence Role constant: relation decoding was reliable when both relations served as oddballs, but significantly weaker when they served as standards. Same/different decoding at the oddballs generalised to shapes and colours withheld from classifier training and was not explained by stimulus familiarity. These findings show that the brain implicitly registers same and different relations at an abstract level that generalises across different instantiations of these relations, and that this information is expressed most strongly when a given relation differs from its established context.

papers.title: TAOK1 restrains cerebral cortex size and determines neural progenitor fate through YAP1 suppression
papers.abstract: The size and complexity of the human cerebral cortex results from precisely coordinated neural progenitor expansion, differentiation, and fate trajectories for which the controlling molecular programs are not well understood. Pathogenic missense and deletion variants in the protein kinase TAOK1 cause a neurodevelopmental disorder characterized by intellectual disability and macrocephaly. We generated human cortical organoids harboring catalytically-inactive TAOK1 disease variant and utilized quantitative phosphoproteomics along with single-cell transcriptomics to uncover disease mechanisms. Catalytically-inactive TAOK1 increases neural progenitor proliferation, accelerates cortical organoid growth, and alters the diversity of cortical cell-types. Phosphoproteomic analyses revealed impaired Hippo signaling with reduced inhibitory phosphorylation of YAP1 concomitant with its sustained nuclear accumulation and activation of TEAD dependent transcription. Progenitors derived from a patient with heterozygous TAOK1 deletion also accumulate nuclear YAP1, extending this finding to a distinct clinical disease-associated TAOK1 lesion. Single-cell transcriptomics demonstrate premature emergence of astrocytic and inhibitory neuronal populations in mutant organoids. Pharmacological inhibition of YAP-TEAD signaling reduced cyclin-A2 labeling and suppressed perturbed Hippo pathway targets. These findings identify TAOK1 as a molecular brake on human cortical overgrowth, implicate previously unrecognized role for Hippo dysfunction in macrocephaly, and reveal pathogenic consequences of accelerated progenitor cycling for both progenitor expansion and fate.

papers.title: Alpha-synuclein overexpression induces sex-dependent alterations in striatal autophagic-lysosomal markers in a Parkinson's disease mouse model
papers.abstract: Parkinson's disease (PD) is characterized by pathological alpha-synuclein (-syn) accumulation and alterations in autophagy. While biological sex is increasingly recognized as a modifier of PD susceptibility and pathophysiology, its relationship with striatal autophagic-lysosomal alterations remains incompletely understood. In this study, we investigated sex-dependent changes in related molecular markers in a mouse model overexpressing -syn. Male and female C57BL/6J mice received bilateral intranigral injections of adeno-associated viral vectors encoding mutant A53T -syn or empty vectors. Dorsal striatal tissue from 29 animals was analyzed at 60 or 120 days post-injection. Confocal imaging of LC3B (microtubule-associated protein 1 light chain 3 beta; autophagosome marker) and LAMP1 (lysosomal-associated membrane protein 1; lysosomal marker) immunofluorescence quantified marker-positive areas, puncta densities, and colocalization. Associations with -syn immunoreactivity, striatal dopaminergic innervation, and axonopathy severity were also examined. At 60 days, no vector-related differences in autophagic-lysosomal markers were detected. However, at 120 days, vector x sex interactions were identified for LC3-positive area, LAMP1-positive area, and LC3 puncta density. Post-hoc comparisons showed reductions in all three measures in -syn males relative to male controls, whereas the corresponding comparisons in females were not significant. After adjustment for striatal -syn immunoreactivity, -syn males had lower LC3- and LAMP1-positive areas, LC3-LAMP1 colocalization area, and LAMP1 puncta density than -syn females. Across -syn mice, greater LAMP1 puncta density was associated with more advanced axonopathy after adjustment for sex and time. These findings identify sex-dependent alterations in striatal autophagic-lysosomal markers following A53T -syn overexpression and suggest an association between lysosomal organization and axonopathy severity. They also underscore the importance of considering biological sex in studies of PD pathophysiology and when evaluating therapies targeting protein clearance pathways.

papers.title: Disrupting translation in CA1 pyramidal cells blocks novelty-induced increases in population firing rate while preserving newly formed assemblies
papers.abstract: Long-term memory depends upon the translation of the plasticity-related proteins required for synaptic consolidation. Whether learning-related changes in hippocampal CA1 coding and synchrony require local synaptic consolidation or reflect plasticity elsewhere remains unknown. We used the inducible protein kinase R (iPKR) chemogenetic system to downregulate cap-dependent translation in CaMKII-expressing dorsal CA1 neurons through intracerebral infusion of an actuator that activates the integrated stress response. Without chemogenetic activation, iPKR mice exhibited elevated pyramidal cell firing and reduced interneuron firing relative to wild-type mice. Infusion of the chemogenetic actuator suppressed c-Fos expression for at least 24 hours and blocked the novelty-related increase in firing observed following vehicle infusion. Nevertheless, other aspects of experience-dependent physiology persisted. Pyramidal cells active during novel exploration remained preferentially recruited into sharp-wave ripples (SPW-Rs) hours into a post-exposure consolidation period. Pairwise coincident activity patterns formed during novel exploration were also reactivated during SPW-Rs with magnitudes and temporal persistence comparable to vehicle sessions and wild-type mice without infusions. When mice returned five hours after exposure to a novel environment, the assemblies formed during translation disruption were also re-expressed at magnitudes comparable to those observed during repeated familiar-environment visits and following novel exploration under vehicle. These findings demonstrate that experience-dependent reorganization of CA1 pyramidal cell synchrony can survive disruption of plasticity-related protein production, whereas novelty-related changes in excitability are impaired. Therefore, SPW-R reactivation and cell assembly consolidation likely depend upon plasticity pathways outside of the eIF2-dependent signaling pathways in the CA1 pyramidal cells targeted by the iPKR system.

papers.title: Single-molecule motion profiling reveals direct and indirect effects of PolyQ expansion on huntingtin dynamics and molecular engagement
papers.abstract: Huntingtons disease (HD) is caused by CAG expansion in HTT, but how PolyQ expansion alters huntingtin behaviour in human neurons remains unclear. We combined live single-molecule imaging and tracking with transformer-based motion profiling to resolve full-length HTT dynamics in pluripotent hESCs and their derived cortical- and MSN-like neurons. HTT occupied three behavioural states: bound, confined, and exploratory. PolyQ expansion progressively shifted molecules from bound and confined states toward the exploratory state. These effects emerged at shorter PolyQ lengths in MSN-like neurons, and only at 150Q included faster exploratory diffusion and impaired return to stable bound or confined states. Tag-swap experiments showed that mt- HTT imposed similar defects on co-expressed wild-type HTT (wt-HTT), revealing a dominant effect of the HD mutation on wt-HTT dynamics. Loss of HTT (HTT-/-) or expression of mt-HTT also altered kinesin and myosin dynamics, consistent with changes in the intracellular environment of HD cells. Thus, PolyQ-expanded HTT does not merely acquire abnormal dynamics, it leads to a broader disruption of the cytoplasmic environment in which both wt-HTT and molecular motors operate.

papers.title: The body as a network, rhythm as the principle: a FREQ-NESS analysis of human movement
papers.abstract: Humans spontaneously move together to rhythm, yet how the body organizes its movements is poorly understood and determining which aspects of this organization support interpersonal coordination requires state-of-the-art analysis methods. By applying for the first time Frequency-resolved Network Estimation via Source Separation (FREQ-NESS) to movement data, we reveal a rhythmic architecture of human movement and show how it shapes coordination between individuals. Using full-body motion capture from dancing dyads, we identify a small set of frequency-specific bodily networks whose organization follows a harmonic hierarchy centred on the musical beat. These networks exhibit distinct spatial configurations, revealing how different rhythmic timescales recruit different patterns of bodily movement. Crucially, not all rhythmic networks contribute equally to interpersonal coordination. The beat emerges as a prominent timescale at which bodily organization and social coordination converge. Shared music primarily enhances the temporal alignment of movement dynamics, whereas visual contact additionally promotes similarity in the bodily configurations expressed by partners, with particularly clear effects at the beat. Together, these findings suggest that interpersonal coordination does not arise from rhythmic movement indiscriminately, but from the engagement of specific rhythmic modes within a structured bodily system. By linking the organization of individual movement to coordination between people, our findings establish a framework for understanding how rhythm connects bodily dynamics and social interaction.

papers.title: The degree of Amyloid β pathology determines the impact of autophagy deficiency
papers.abstract: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is characterized by amyloid {beta} (A{beta}) deposition, tau aggregation and impaired proteostasis, including autophagy dysfunction. However, how autophagy deficiency affects A{beta} pathology and disease progression remains unclear. We crossed excitatory neuronspecific Atg7 knockout mice with App knock-in mice (AppNL-F/NL-F and AppNL-G-F/NL-G-F) and assessed A{beta} pathology, extracellular vesicle (EV) release, cognition, gamma oscillatory activity, cell death, brain atrophy and proteomic changes. Autophagy deficiency reduced extracellular A{beta} plaque burden despite increased release of A{beta}-containing EVs. Notably, combined Arctic-A{beta} pathology and autophagy deficiency impaired gamma oscillatory activity, behaviour and memory, activated cell death signalling and shortened lifespan. CA1 proteomics identified a voltage-gated potassium channel subunit markedly increased upon Atg7 deletion. Surprisingly, less pronounced A{beta} pathology counteracted several detrimental effects, potentially through improved cellular transport and reduced protein translation. These findings reveal that autophagy regulates A{beta} metabolism and that A{beta} pathology severity determines the consequences of autophagy deficiency, highlighting autophagy modulation as a context-dependent therapeutic target in AD.

papers.title: One genome, two connectomes: genetic encoding of synapse drive to specify environment-appropriate wiring
papers.abstract: The form of neural wiring must be robust as well as appropriate for the environment. In resource-rich environments, C. elegans larvae rapidly mature into reproductive adults; otherwise, they enter dauer diapause, a state with altered physiology and behaviors for survival and dispersal from harsh environments. By comparing the electron microscopic reconstruction of multiple dauers and non-dauers, we define two consensus connectomes that stereotypically differ in approximately 1/3 wiring partnerships. We show that these wiring differences result from changes in the availability and selectivity of neurite neighbors to form synapses, as well as how strongly wiring partners choose to connect. We further demonstrate that these changes are best quantified by synapse drive, represented as the density of synapses on available contact, and a pair of synapse drive changes have behavioral consequences. We propose that a connectome results from environment-informed genetic specification of synapse drive, the principal determinant of wiring partnership, among available neurite neighbors.

papers.title: Instruction Timing Governs Representational Competition in Behavioral Timescale Synaptic Plasticity
papers.abstract: Neurons can form new representations within a single experience through behavioral-timescale synaptic plasticity (BTSP), yet how such rapid learning affects previously established representations remains unclear. We present an analytically tractable theory of BTSP, constrained by experimental measurements in hippocampal CA1, to examine how successive learning events interact within individual neurons. Competition between temporally narrow potentiation and broader, weight-dependent depression generates nonmonotonic interference as a function of the separation between instructive events. Nearby events merge representations, intermediate separations produce the strongest suppression and overwriting, and distant events allow coexistence. This interference arises from the distinct timescales of potentiation and depression rather than the precise functional form of the plasticity kernel. Analytically derived synaptic-weight covariances identify the origin of this constructive-destructive interaction, and a quantitative phase diagram predicts how the transitions between regimes depend on running speed and the spatial tuning of presynaptic inputs. The theory further identifies a velocity-dependent exclusion zone in which the coexistence of distinct representations is strongly suppressed. The effects of new learning therefore depend not only on the animal's current running speed but also on the pre-existing tuning width of presynaptic inputs. Our theory thus predicts the conditions under which new hippocampal place fields merge with, overwrite, or preserve existing representations.

papers.title: Neuronal heparan sulfate controls the brain accumulation and glymphatic clearance of pathogenic α-synuclein
papers.abstract: In Parkinson's disease and dementia with Lewy bodies, fibrillar aggregates of the -synuclein (-syn) protein are released into the extracellular space and drive disease progression, yet the mechanisms governing their in vivo neuronal uptake and clearance remain poorly understood. Heparan sulfate proteoglycans (HSPGs) act as receptors for -syn fibril internalization in iPSC-derived dopaminergic neurons and could therefore advance synucleinopathy progression in patients. Here we show that -syn fibrils interact electrostatically with the sulfate groups in the HS chains with high affinity, and that genetically reducing the sulfation of neuronal HS reduces the accumulation of -syn aggregates in multiple brain areas, the loss of dopaminergic neurons, and the development of a locomotor behavioral phenotype in mice intracerebrally injected with -syn recombinant fibrils (PFFs). In vivo imaging revealed that HS is also a molecular obstacle to the glymphatic clearance of -syn fibrils, as radiolabeled -syn PFFs travel faster through the brain towards cerebrospinal clearance in mice with less sulfated neuronal HS than in wild-type mice. Collectively, this study provides in vivo evidence that neuronal HS accelerates -syn pathology, potentially by promoting neuronal uptake while slowing the glymphatic clearance of -syn fibrils and, therefore, is a promising therapeutic target to halt synucleinopathies.

papers.title: Modeling Speech-in-Noise Performance Using an Auditory-Nerve Manifold
papers.abstract: Speech-in-noise difficulties often exceed audiometric profile-based predictions, suggesting suprathreshold neural coding deficits limit understanding even when audibility is preserved. A major limitation of clinical speech tests is that reduced performance can reflect either hair-cell loss or cochlear neural degeneration (CND). We propose a computational framework estimating each factor relative contribution at a population level. We simulated auditory-nerve responses to a consonant-identification task for 94 adults (19-83 years; pure-tone average (PTA) 0-55 dB HL) under three conditions: audiometric loss alone, CND affecting low- and medium-spontaneous-rate (LS and MS) fibers, and CND affecting all fiber types. A convolutional autoencoder was used to learn low-dimensional embeddings from neurograms, and downstream classifiers were used to perform consonant identification from the embeddings. We found that audiometric loss alone, and CND of LS and MS fibers consistently produced mismatch between model and human accuracies, whereas CND affecting all fiber types predicted human accuracy closely (mean absolute error (MAE) = 0.089, r = 0.81, rho = 0.83) on an individual level, while capturing the broad structure of human confusions.

papers.title: Human lipidomics guides brain-inspired lipoprotein particle approach to ameliorate Alzheimer's disease pathology
papers.abstract: APOE encodes the principal lipid-transporting protein in the brain, and lipid dysregulation is increasingly implicated in Alzheimer's disease (AD) pathogenesis. The APOE4 allele, together with advanced age and female sex, are major risk factors for late-onset AD. Yet how these risk factors interact to reshape lipid composition and transport in the brain remains unclear. Herein, we characterize lipidomic profiles in the brain, cerebrospinal fluid (CSF), and blood of individuals with or without AD, as well as of mice expressing humanized APOE. We identify brain lipidomic shifts associated with AD in humans, including relative depletion of highly unsaturated lipids, with many changes resembling those associated with APOE4 alone. Individuals with AD show striking depletion of lipoprotein particle (LP)-associated lipid abundance in the CSF. Additionally, humanized APOE4 mice exhibit an age-dependent deficit in CSF LP-associated lipid abundance relative to APOE3 mice. Accordingly, we leverage these insights to engineer brain-inspired reconstituted LPs (rLPs) with the goal of restoring lipid transport in the brain. rLPs promote cholesterol efflux from human induced pluripotent stem cell-derived APOE4 astrocytes in vitro. In an AD mouse model (5xFAD) expressing humanized APOE4, these nanoparticles reduce lipid-droplet accumulation, facilitate amyloid-beta clearance, enhance synaptic integrity, and improve cognitive function. Together, our results provide a resource mapping lipidomic changes across the Alzheimer's risk triad and demonstrate that engineered rLPs can counter lipid accumulation and associated pathology in the brain, and cognitive deficits in vivo.

papers.title: Non-invasive Topographic Sculpting of the Mammalian Auditory Cortex with Low-intensity Focused Ultrasound: A Platform for Personalized Editing of Sensory Representations
papers.abstract: Background: Topographic maps organize the mammalian cortex, and their maladaptive reorganization underlies conditions like chronic tinnitus and focal dystonia. Low-intensity focused ultrasound (FUS) produces offline neuromodulation, yet its submillimeter spatial distribution within sensory maps remains poorly understood. Objective: To determine how offline FUS-induced amplitude changes are spatially organized within the mouse primary auditory cortex (A1) tonotopic map and depend on sonication intensity. Methods: Widefield Ca2+ imaging was combined with phased-array FUS (750 kHz, <1.5 W/cm2 Isppa, no microbubbles) in Thy1-GCaMP6s x CBA/CaJ mice. Twenty-second sonication was steered to each animal's tone-evoked centroid at 0.625 or 1.2 W/cm2. Offline gain was quantified over 40 min using Euclidean distance from the focus and functional distance (first principal component, PC1, percentile brackets). Results: Modulation followed functional rather than physical geometry: effects appeared isotropic in Euclidean distance but varied spatially across functional brackets, peaking 10 min post-sonication and persisting upwards of 40 min. Both intensities carved a modulatory trough between the 50th and 70th percentiles of A1's sensory representation (~1.0-1.2 mm from target). At 0.625 W/cm2 Isppa, this trough became suppressive (gain < 1.0) and shifted relative response timing across cortical fields, an effect absent at 1.2 W/cm2. Conclusions: Offline FUS modulation in A1 is organized by functional topography rather than physical distance, demonstrating that low-intensity FUS can serve as a spatially constrained suppressant. A forward-projection model built on this profile provides a quantitative basis for personalized, coordinate-based sonication planning for focal sensory pathologies like tinnitus.

papers.title: Neuronal Culture Media Shape Protein Abundance and Turnover in Human iPSC-Derived Neurons
papers.abstract: Cultured neuron models are essential for studying neuronal biology and disease, yet it remains unclear how neuronal culture media shape the global proteome and protein turnover. Here, we compared human iPSC-derived neurons cultured in four different media: BrainPhys, DMEM/F-12, Neurobasal, or a 1:1 DMEM/F-12:Neurobasal mixture using label-free and dynamic SILAC proteomics. To enable protein turnover measurements in BrainPhys, we developed an in-house SILAC-compatible BrainPhys formulation that supported comparable viability and proteome coverage to commercial BrainPhys. BrainPhys produced a proteome and turnover landscape distinct from the other three media, which closely resembled one another. BrainPhys-cultured neurons showed lower relative abundance of DNA replication- and progenitor-associated proteins and higher relative abundance of synaptic and neuronal projection proteins, consistent with a more mature neuronal proteome. BrainPhys also globally prolonged protein half-lives, yielding a turnover profile more similar to later-stage primary neurons and in vivo brain. Despite their distinct basal proteomes, neurons cultured in different media exhibited a conserved proteomic response to acute lysosomal inhibition. Bafilomycin A1 treatment increased the relative abundance and synthesis of autophagy-associated proteins while decreasing the relative abundance of lysosomal hydrolases. Together, these findings identify neuronal culture medium as a critical determinant of neuronal proteome composition and dynamics and establish a SILAC-compatible BrainPhys formulation for future studies of neuronal proteostasis.

papers.title: Target-dependent modulation of finely tuned gamma by transcranial ultrasound in Parkinson's disease
papers.abstract: Background: Finely tuned gamma (FTG) is a narrowband oscillation associated with dopaminergic ON states and dyskinesia in Parkinson's disease (PD), although its physiological significance remains debated. While deep brain stimulation (DBS) can entrain gamma oscillations, whether noninvasive ultrasound can modulate endogenous FTG across motor circuits remains unclear. Methods: We analyzed local field potentials recorded using sensing-enabled DBS systems in two cohorts of patients: 17 with subthalamic nucleus (STN) and 10 with globus pallidus internus (GPi) electrodes. Theta-burst transcranial ultrasound stimulation (tbTUS) targeted the primary motor cortex (M1) or GPi. FTG was assessed before, during, and up to 45 minutes after sonication. Associations with beta activity, levodopa-equivalent daily dose (LEDD), and dyskinesia were also examined. Results: FTG was detected in eight STN patients and one GPi patient, with five exhibiting reproducible peaks suitable for longitudinal analysis, broadly consistent with previous reports of intermittent FTG expression. M1 sonication reduced STN FTG in three patients, whereas GPi sonication increased STN FTG in one but did not significantly alter locally recorded GPi FTG in another. Finger-tapping-related FTG responses were heterogeneous. Resting FTG was not significantly correlated with beta activity or LEDD. However, dyskinesia was more frequent in sessions with detectable FTG than in those without (47% vs. 20%), although this association was not statistically significant (p = 0.067). Conclusions: These findings suggest that noninvasive ultrasound can modulate endogenous FTG in a circuit-dependent manner, distinct from DBS-induced gamma entrainment. FTG may provide a complementary electrophysiological biomarker alongside beta oscillations, potentially capturing additional aspects of motor-network activity and dyskinesia. Combining noninvasive TUS with intracranial DBS sensing may offer a useful approach for investigating FTG and its potential application in future adaptive DBS and individualized neuromodulation strategies.

papers.title: Exposure-driven modulation of neural response to novel word forms in toddlers
papers.abstract: An enhancement of an early brain signal in response to novel word forms has been associated with lexical learning in adults. Here, we measured neural responses to novel pseudowords in 24-month-olds to investigate whether a similar early modulation occurs in young children. Participants were presented with familiar French words (e.g., bateau, boat) and novel pseudowords (e.g., bamon). Event-related potentials were time-locked to the word disambiguation point (i.e., the onset of the second syllable) and analyzed across three time bins (4 minutes each) during the experiment. We observed an early positive response, P100, occurring around 100 ms after the word disambiguation point, which decreased for pseudowords over the course of repeated exposure. No such amplitude change was observed for familiar words. These results demonstrate an early reduction in neural responses to novel word forms, suggesting rapid and dynamic changes in brain activity associated with the familiarization of novel lexical items.

papers.title: Prior Experience Alters Exploration in Standard Behavioral Assays More Robustly Than Sex or Light/Dark Cycle in C57BL/6J Mice
papers.abstract: Circadian phase during testing, biological sex, and repeated exposure to the same testing apparatus are all experimental variables known to impact outcomes in neurobehavioral studies. However, the combined, interactive effects of these intrinsic and extrinsic variables on common behavioral tests are not well established, and the effect of repeated testing is particularly understudied. In this study, we examined the compounding impact of these variables by comparing male and female mice on either a standard light cycle or reversed light cycle in the elevated plus maze (EPM), elevated zero maze (EZM), open field test (OFT), Y-maze spontaneous alternation (SA), and novel object recognition (NOR). To examine the impact of repeated exposure to the same testing apparatus, mice were re-exposed to the EPM, EZM, OFT and SA 24 hours after the initial test. We found that exploratory behavior in EPM, EZM, and OFT was robustly diminished on the second exposure. Furthermore, exploration in the open arms of the EPM dropped dramatically, proportionally more than can be explained by the drop in total exploration. The only endpoint unaffected by repeated testing was percent alternation in SA. Light cycle had smaller, more inconsistent effects across assays; male mice on a reversed light-dark cycle showed increased object exploration and improved discrimination in NOR, and mice on a reversed light-dark cycle showed less time exploring the center in the OFT. The effect of sex was minimal, and behavior in EZM and Y-maze was unaffected by sex or light condition. We propose that the first test in any assay elicits an incidental learning experience which is expressed on the second test as a reduction in exploration. The robustness of this test-retest drop in exploration argues that this is a critical experimental variable that must be incorporated into experimental design and interpretation of behavioral results.

papers.title: Assessing gait control from short time series using a geometric characterization of stride-by-stride corrections
papers.abstract: Gait variability in healthy adults exhibits Long-Range Autocorrelations (LRA), reflecting long-term statistical dependencies between stride intervals. Previous studies have interpreted LRA within an optimal control framework, where stride length and duration are regulated in a coordinated manner to maintain a constant walking speed. Such objective offers redundancy among gait parameters that achieve success. In this context, imposing constraints on the walking cadence reduces this redundancy and leads to a loss of LRA. The model therefore predicts that during free walking, stride-by-stride adjustments should be directed toward the redundant axis, whereas during cued walking, they should be directed toward the imposed target values. Consequently, differences between conditions should be observable based on a geometric characterization of changes in length and duration. With simulations and experimental data, we show that stride-by-stride adjustments discriminate between cued and free walking conditions, supporting the geometric interpretation of the model. Moreover, this metric achieves good discrimination (Area Under the Curve = 0.74) for 50-stride series, compared with LRA estimates that typically require series of 80 strides to achieve comparable success. In sum, our study validates a novel geometric approach to quantifying gait control strategies, supporting the emergence of LRA through flexible adjustments of stride parameters.

papers.title: Contextual Guidance and Suppression in Visual Search: Probing Learned Attentional Settings With a Color Singleton
papers.abstract: How does learning a spatial context shape the selection of a newly salient distractor? In two eye-tracking experiments (26 participants each), observers searched for a T among Ls in repeated (Old) or novel (New) configurations. A designated distractor occupied a fixed or variable location and became a red color singleton in the second session. Repeated configurations predicted a stable target location in Experiment 1 but not in Experiment 2. Familiar configurations yielded faster responses alongside an increased probability of initial saccades toward fixed-location singletons. These co-occurring effects were observed at outer singleton locations in Experiment 1 and at both inner and outer locations in Experiment 2. Contextual cueing was stronger in Experiment 1, where familiar configurations also increased initial target selection, reduced ordinary-distractor selection, and facilitated target acquisition. These findings suggest that learned context shapes both the priority assigned to individual search items and search efficiency following distractor selection. The singleton probe reveals how learned spatial contexts shape both the distribution of attentional priority across individual search items and the efficiency of search following distractor selection.

papers.title: Network size regulates the balance between reuse and reconstruction of neural dynamics during reversal learning
papers.abstract: Neural system size is a fundamental quantitative property that may influence cognitive function. While larger neural systems have been associated with enhanced cognitive performance, how system size contributes to cognitive flexibility remains poorly understood. In particular, it is unclear whether size influences not only how efficiently a system learns but also how previously established neural dynamics are reorganized when learned associations must change. We addressed this question using recurrent neural networks trained on a reversal learning task. Despite reaching the same performance criterion, networks differed strikingly in how their internal dynamics changed across reversal. Some networks largely preserved prereversal population trajectories, thereby reusing previously established dynamics, whereas others substantially reorganized them, effectively reconstructing their dynamical structure. This continuum of adaptation strategies was particularly broad in small networks. Importantly, the extent of reorganization was related to network properties established before reversal: networks with larger prereversal recurrent weights tended to exhibit stronger reconstruction. We then examined whether the balance between reuse and reconstruction depended systematically on network size. As network size increased, changes in internal dynamics became progressively smaller and less variable, indicating increasing convergence toward the reuse strategy. Larger networks also learned both the initial and reversed mappings more rapidly and consistently. Thus, network size shapes not only learning efficiency but also the strategy by which previously learned population dynamics are modified during flexible adaptation, shifting the balance from diverse reuse reconstruction strategies in small networks toward consistent reuse in larger networks.

papers.title: A Spatiotemporal Code for Cognitive Flexibility in the Mid-Posterior Cerebellar Cortex
papers.abstract: Cognitive flexibility is the critical ability to adapt behavior in changing environments. Although traditionally associated with the prefrontal cortex, behavioral, lesion, and functional imaging evidence suggests the cerebellum contributes to cognitive flexibility. To test the role of the cerebellum at the circuit level, we paired widefield calcium imaging of single-cell Purkinje cells with a cognitive flexibility task and computational behavioral model. We find mid-posterior Purkinje cells encode all reinforcement learning parameters needed to produce flexible behavior, including specific representations for contingency degradation (CD) and enhancement (CE). Comparing somatic and dendritic encoding reveals a significant bias towards integrative multi-trial CD and CE representations in somas over long timescales, while dendrites encode more single-trial reward prediction errors. Activating lobule VIa, the region with strongest CD flexibility encoding, with patterned photostimulation causally expedites CD behavior. These results establish that the cerebellum extends beyond its canonical motoric functions to act as an important coordinator of cognitive flexibility behavior.

papers.title: Non-Ordinary Visual Spaces, Self-Motion and Sense of Agency in Near-Death Experiences
papers.abstract: Near-death experiences (NDEs) are a subset of non-ordinary states consciousness in which people frequently report unusual perceptions of space and self-motion. How the occurrence of self-motion varies across the visual-field boundary configurations described in first-person accounts remains underinvestigated. Alongside a semi-structured digital questionnaire, participants represented their NDE visual spaces schematically, outlining visual-field boundaries and marking self-location and self-motion direction. Across successive reconstructions, we examined visual-field geometry and extent in relation to self-location, the subjective experience of where one feels located, and self-motion, the perceived movement of the self through visual space. In spaces with reported self-motion, we also examined whether the movement was experienced as voluntarily initiated or controlled. Self-motion predominated in conical visual fields and in fields bounded by more strongly curved elliptic arcs. Self-motion was absent in most fields bounded by flatter elliptic arcs and in most fully ellipsoidal fields. Among spaces with self-motion, passive agency predominated in conical fields. Active agency was more frequent in ellipsoidal than in conical fields and was reported in half of the fully ellipsoidal fields with self-motion. Sparse data limited these exploratory comparisons. The analysis yielded no clear evidence of an association between perceived velocity magnitude and agency. These findings suggest that visual-field geometry is associated with whether self-motion occurs during the NDE Core and, when it occurs, with whether it is experienced as voluntarily initiated or controlled. The reconstruction approach provides a framework for investigating the spatial organization of first-person experience in NDEs.

papers.title: Ultra-Fast Signals during Spreading Depolarizations
papers.abstract: Spreading depolarizations (SDs) are major pathophysiological events implicated in various brain diseases. Hallmarks of SD include a negative DC shift, reflecting near-complete neuronal depolarization, and the depression of cortical activity. Using microelectrode field potential recordings from the rat cortex, we found that, in contrast to the depression of activity in conventional AC frequency bands (0.5-1000 Hz), high-potassium-induced SDs were associated with increased local field potential power at ultra-fast frequencies (4-8 kHz), which we term the Ultra-Fast Signal (UFS). UFSs were time-locked to the SD-related DC shifts, although their peaks were delayed relative to those of the DC shifts. Furthermore, UFS magnitude and duration correlated with those of the DC shift, and UFSs exhibited vertical propagation profiles across cortical depth similar to DC shifts. During partial superficial SDs, UFSs were confined to the cortical layers recruited by the SD. UFSs were also prominent in SD clusters during isoelectric SDs, occurring against a background of suppressed AC activity. We propose that the UFS could serve as an additional SD marker that is particularly useful for detecting isoelectric SDs.

papers.title: A Cross-Tissue Multi-Omics Atlas of Brain Transcriptomes and Liquid Biopsy EV Proteomes in Parkinson's Disease and Multiple System Atrophy
papers.abstract: Parkinson's disease (PD) and Multiple System Atrophy (MSA) are progressive synucleinopathies characterized by widespread molecular alterations across neuronal and glial populations. While brain tissue provides direct insight into disease mechanisms, liquid biopsies, particularly extracellular vesicles (EVs) in plasma, cerebrospinal fluid (CSF), and urine, offer a minimally invasive avenue for clinical diagnosis and monitoring. However, the extent to which cell-type-specific brain transcriptional changes translate into detectable circulating protein signatures remains unclear. Here, we present a comprehensive multi-omics meta-analysis integrating eight human post-mortem brain single-nucleus RNA-sequencing (snRNA-seq) datasets with eight circulating proteomic datasets. We uniformly reprocessed and analyzed over 1 million nuclei, spanning ~20,000 protein-coding genes across four broadly defined disease-relevant brain regions from 171 individuals alongside ~8,000 liquid biopsy proteins from over 400 individuals. We resolved cell-type-specific differentially expressed genes (DEGs) across dopaminergic neurons, microglia, astrocytes, and oligodendrocytes alongside disease-specific differentially expressed proteins (DEPs) in peripheral biofluids. Mapping brain DEGs onto liquid biopsy proteomes revealed that ~25% of brain DEGs were detectable as biofluid DEPs in at least one dataset, while multi-cohort filtering prioritized 32 unique recurrent cross-omic biomarkers. These include concordantly regulated markers of complement and glial reactivity (C1QB, C3, CHI3L1), neurotrophic and neuropeptide signaling (IGFBP5, NRP1, SST), lipid metabolism (LPL, APOC1), proteostasis (HSP90B1), and cytoskeletal/extracellular matrix remodeling (MMP2, PLOD1), alongside inversely regulated chaperones and synaptic/vascular factors (HSP90AA1, CAMK2A, VWF). Furthermore, cross-omic protein-protein interaction networks converged on pathways governing chaperone-mediated protein folding, ubiquitin-proteasome degradation, mitochondrial bioenergetics, and SNARE-mediated vesicular transport. Ultimately, this integrative atlas links brain cell-type-specific transcriptomic dysregulation to accessible EV cargo, providing a scalable framework for mechanistically informed liquid biopsies in neurodegeneration.

papers.title: Repeated transcranial ultrasound is associated with altered temporal organization of spontaneous wheel activity during sleep disruption in mice
papers.abstract: Background: Motor-cortex-targeted transcranial ultrasound stimulation (tUS) can influence neural activity and motor responses, but its relationship to spontaneous behavior during sleep disruption (SD) remains unclear. Objective: To examine how repeated tUS during sustained SD relates to the temporal organization of spontaneous running and inactivity bouts. Methods: We recorded wheel activity in 36 mice for 17 days. On Days 13-17, mice in control (Ctrl) or wheel-confinement SD housing received bilateral motor-cortex-targeted tUS or sham. Another 32 mice followed the same treatment schedule and completed the retention phase of the novel object recognition test before open-field testing on Day 17. EEG/EMG recordings in 11 untreated mice characterized the SD sleep-wake phenotype. Hydrophone measurements in water and simulations using individual skull models characterized acoustic exposure. Results: During the final three dark phases, SD/tUS mice had lower activity-resumption probability (0.132 vs 0.224) and longer median inactivity bouts (3.81 vs 2.48 min) than SD/Sham mice. Both housing-by-treatment interactions were significant. Within SD, neither total rotations nor running intensity differed significantly. The mean discrimination index was higher with tUS, although the Holm-adjusted comparison was nonsignificant. SD/tUS mice spent longer in the open-field center than SD/Sham mice. Across all 32 behavioral-test mice, lower resumption probability and longer pauses correlated with longer center time the next day. Untreated SD mice slept more and had more frequent sleep-wake transitions. Conclusions: During ongoing SD, mice receiving repeated motor-cortex-targeted tUS were less likely than sham-treated mice to resume wheel running. Their longer pauses between runs may provide opportunities for sustained rest.

papers.title: Methamphetamine acute exposure induces mitochondrial fragmentation in ventral tegmental area dopamine neurons
papers.abstract: Methamphetamine (METH) is a potent psychostimulant that primarily acts on the dopaminergic system and has strong reinforcing effects. It also induces oxidative stress, impairs mitochondrial function, and causes neurotoxicity at high doses. We previously showed that long-term METH self-administration increases mitochondrial respiratory metabolism and reduces antioxidant capacity in the mesolimbic dopaminergic circuit. However, the effects of METH exposure on mitochondrial structure in dopamine neurons remained unexplored. Here, we examine the acute effects of METH on mitochondrial morphology using a methodology that combines classical immunofluorescence labeling with advanced computational clearing methods and quantitative morphometric analysis. We administered acute METH treatments to mice at doses known to produce stimulant (3 mg/kg) or neurotoxic (20 mg/kg) effects. One week later, quantitative morphological analysis showed that neurotoxic METH exposure increased mitochondrial fragmentation in tyrosine hydroxylase (TH)-positive dopaminergic neurons, significantly reducing mitochondrial size and length while increasing estimated roundness. By contrast, NeuN-labeled non-dopaminergic VTA neurons showed no changes in mitochondrial morphology, suggesting that acute susceptibility to METH-induced mitochondrial fragmentation is cell-type-specific in dopamine neurons. In addition, dopamine neuron size decreased, particularly after the neurotoxic METH dose. Our findings shed light on the lasting effects of METH exposure on mitochondrial structure and can help explain the early mechanisms underlying mitochondrial functional changes in VTA dopamine neurons.

papers.title: Mechanical role of dural structures and tumor material heterogeneity in brain tumor mass effect
papers.abstract: Brain tumor growth induces considerable deformation of the surrounding tissue, yet the mechanical contribution of intracranial dural structures and the influence of tumor material heterogeneity on mass effect remain poorly understood. In this study, we developed a heterogeneous finite element model of the brain to investigate the mechanical role of the falx cerebri and tentorium cerebelli and to determine how variations in tumor subregion stiffness influence the mechanical response of the brain. Two complementary analyses were performed. First, synthetic lesion models with and without the falx and tentorium were compared under otherwise identical conditions. Inclusion of these structures produced only minor changes in global displacement magnitude, but substantially altered the spatial distribution of stress. The dural structures acted as stiff internal partitions that limited interhemispheric and supratentorial-infratentorial deformation and modified load transmission throughout the brain. Including the dural structures led to a different pattern of ventricular volume change during tumor growth, with both lateral ventricles compressed in the dura-included model, whereas without the dura the ventricle on the tumor side expanded while the opposite ventricle was compressed. Second, a parametric analysis was performed using MRI-informed patient-specific tumors comprising necrotic tumor core (NTC), contrast-enhancing tumor core (ETC), and peritumoral edema (Ed). Variations in ETC stiffness produced the largest and most spatially distributed changes in displacement and von Mises stress, with stronger effects in ETC-dominant tumors. Edema stiffness produced weaker and more diffuse effects, whereas NTC stiffness mainly affected the principal stretch within the tumor. These findings demonstrate that intracranial dural structures alter the distribution of tumor-induced deformation and stress despite their limited influence on global displacement magnitude. In the patient-specific models, varying the tumor stiffness within its reported range changed the mechanical response by only a few percent, with the ETC having the largest influence.

papers.title: SHANK3-actin cytoskeleton coupling regulates nanoscale remodelling of the postsynaptic density
papers.abstract: Dynamic remodelling of multiprotein signalling complexes allows cells to rapidly adapt signalling strength. At synapses, neurotransmitter receptors and scaffolds concentrate in subsynaptic nanoclusters that govern synaptic signalling strength and that are dynamically remodelled by synaptic activity. However, although this distinct nanoscale organization of synaptic protein complexes is well-established, the mechanisms that control the activity-induced reorganization of these complexes remain elusive. Here, to resolve the mechanisms underlying the activity-induced spatiotemporal reorganization of the PSD, we combined CRISPR/Cas9-mediated tagging of endogenous synaptic proteins and quantitative super-resolution microscopy. We found that synaptic potentiation drives a rapid and long-lasting increase in the number and density of PSD scaffold nanoclusters. Strikingly, activity-induced reorganization of scaffold proteins originated in deep PSD layers and preceded AMPA receptor repositioning, indicating that newly recruited receptors populate preformed scaffold nanoclusters. Computational simulations support that this reorganization is sufficient to drive potentiation of synaptic responses. Mechanistically, we found that the interaction between the scaffold SHANK3 and the actin cytoskeleton is essential for activity-induced PSD nanocluster remodelling. Altogether, our findings present a novel mechanism through which cytoskeletal interactions remodel the spatial organization of the PSD, advancing our understanding of how the dynamic nanoscale reorganization of protein complexes can drive neuronal signalling.

papers.title: Functional balance between inhibitory and disinhibitory pathways predicts the heterogeneous effects of arousal on cortical timescales
papers.abstract: Cortical activity exhibits diverse timescales that vary with behavioral state, but the underlying circuit mechanisms remain unclear. Analyzing Allen Institute Neuropixels recordings from mouse primary visual cortex, we found that the fraction of excitatory neurons activated by optogenetic stimulation of somatostatin (SST) interneurons varied across mice. Intrinsic timescales lengthened during arousal in mice with a lower fraction of activated excitatory neurons and shortened in those with a higher fraction. To investigate a possible mechanism, we trained spiking networks with cell-type-specific plasticity, producing configurations dominated by direct SST inhibition of excitatory neurons or indirect disinhibition via parvalbumin interneurons. Arousal-like input to vasoactive intestinal peptide (VIP) interneurons slowed assembly dynamics, lengthened intrinsic timescales, and accelerated assembly formation when direct inhibition dominated, with opposite effects when indirect disinhibition dominated. Our results suggest that the balance between these pathways can account for opposite timescale responses to arousal and shape its computational consequences.

papers.title: Ongoing activity in anatomically recurrent cortex is predominantly feedforward
papers.abstract: The cerebral cortex is the major site of computation in the brain, and its recurrent wiring has motivated models in which repeated neuronal activation maintains information in stable attractor states. Large language models illustrate an alternative principle by transforming information layer by layer during each forward pass. A first step toward understanding what cortex and these models can teach us about each other is to establish whether feedforward dynamics can predominate in recurrent cortex. Here, we show that ongoing activity in the frontal cortex of awake mice is composed of parabolic neuronal avalanches in which activity progresses mainly through newly recruited neurons. Using two-photon calcium imaging in hundreds of simultaneously recorded layer II/III pyramidal neurons, we decomposed avalanche size into the number of participating neurons, mean activations per participant, and mean inferred spikes per activation. Avalanche size grew approximately quadratically with duration up to 0.5 s, primarily through recruitment of additional neurons. Participating neurons contributed close to one spike per avalanche on average. Newly recruited neurons also dominated the rise and fall of the average avalanche profile. An unbiased recruitment model, in which all neurons have the same selection probability, accounted for the predominance of new over repeat participation, showing that feedforward recruitment can dominate even when previously active neurons remain available for reactivation. Parabolic avalanches thus express predominantly feedforward dynamics within anatomically recurrent cortex. Cortical computation may therefore have more in common with feedforward processing in large language models than recurrent anatomy alone would suggest.
